description: Complete menu rules for Indian lunch menu planning — matches old app rule set

rules._comment: nonveg_biryani_once_per_week counts biryani DAYS, so a counter with 2+ nonveg slots could satisfy it by stacking two biryanis onto one day. This caps the dishes per day so the pair is biryani + something else. allowed_day_types keeps the biryani on the biryani day: a 'mix' day is not narrowed by the theme filter at all, so without this a themed counter could serve biryani on Monday and none on its actual biryani day. A counter themed biryani every weekday is unaffected (every day is an allowed day).
rules.name: nonveg_biryani_one_per_day

rules._comment: The 15-day rolling window behind special_sambar_weekly (rulebook 82). The weekly max caps it within a plan; this reads saved history so a special sambar served last week is held off until the 15 days clear.
rules.name: special_sambar_15d_window

rules._comment: The veg plate must not echo itself. veg_gravy and veg_dry together may not serve the same key ingredient on one day — a paneer gravy beside a paneer dry is legal under every other rule (different course_type, different colour, different texture) and reads as one dish served twice. HARD, and measured as feasible on all 78 counters that run either slot before it was written: every one can give each veg cell a distinct named key ingredient. Scoped to these two slots on purpose. Plate-wide is the reading that sounds right and cannot be built — `nonveg_main` carries six distinct key ingredients in the whole ontology against a mandated daily chicken gravy, `dal`'s value is literally `dal` on all 59 counters, `bread`'s is `wheat` on 64 and `rice`'s is `mixed_vegetables` on 61. In those slots the key ingredient is the slot's identity, not a variety dimension. `require_value` keeps blank-key_ingredient dishes out of these two pools, without which the rule is worse than nothing: a blank is unconstrained, so the solver would escape it by serving exactly the dishes nobody has classified.
rules.name: veg_plate_distinct_key_ingredient

rules._comment: And it must not come straight back: three CLEAR days before a key ingredient returns to the same slot, so a carrot gravy on Monday means no carrot gravy until Friday. `per_base_slot` keeps the gravy answering to other gravies and the dry to other dries — pooling them would be the plate-wide ban above, which cannot be built. Auto-relaxes per slot when the pool cannot supply a distinct value for every cell in the window, so a thin slot degrades and reports instead of taking the plan down.
rules.name: veg_key_ingredient_three_day_gap

rules._comment: The rest of the plate, softly. Any key ingredient appearing on two cells of ONE day is penalised across every slot — a paneer gravy beside a paneer starter, or carrot in the gravy and the salad. SOFT rather than hard because the slots this reaches include the ones whose ingredient IS their identity: chicken must be able to outbid it on a non-veg counter, and wheat on a bread slot. `scope: day` is what makes it see a plate at all; the default horizon scope collapses a value to one bool per day and structurally cannot.
rules.name: plate_key_ingredient_echo

rules._comment: The veg plate must not echo its PROTEIN either. veg_gravy and veg_dry may not serve the same primary_protein on one day: a soya chaap gravy beside a soya keema dry is one idea served twice, and the client named exactly that case. This is the second half of a pair with veg_plate_distinct_key_ingredient -- the two columns disagree often enough to need both, e.g. 121 Bangalore rows carry primary_protein soy against 98 carrying key_ingredient soy, so 23 soya dishes are invisible to the key_ingredient rule. Measured feasible on all 70 counters running 2+ veg cells before it was written. Deliberately NO require_value, which is the opposite call from the key_ingredient rule and for a real reason: a blank key_ingredient is an UNCLASSIFIED dish (a gap in the data the solver would escape into), while a blank primary_protein means NO PROTEIN FOCUS -- it is the value the enriched workbooks wrote as literal 'none' and merge_enriched_ontology folds to blank. Two plain vegetable dishes are not a repeat, so blanks are unconstrained here by design, and dropping them would delete 56% of veg_gravy and 74% of veg_dry.
rules.name: veg_plate_distinct_protein

rules._comment: And softly across the whole plate: any protein on two cells of ONE day is penalised -- a paneer gravy beside a paneer starter, soya in the rice and again in the veg dry. SOFT, not hard, because this reaches nonveg_main, whose protein is 0% blank and where nonveg_main_daily_pair mandates a chicken gravy every day: on a 2-cell non-veg station a second chicken dish is often forced, and chicken has to be able to outbid this. scope:day is what makes it see a plate at all -- the default horizon scope collapses a value to one bool per day and structurally cannot. PRIORITY is medium, not high, and the reason is note 32 rather than the client's emphasis: the theme tier is already measurably inverted at MAX_NUM_DAYS, a fifth high-tier soft rule widens that, and the firm half of this requirement is already carried by veg_plate_distinct_protein, which is a HARD constraint and so outranks every soft tier regardless. What stays soft here is the 'and everywhere else on the plate too' part, which is exactly the thing that should yield to a real rule.
rules.name: plate_protein_echo

rules._comment: ...and across the week, more gently. A protein appearing on two DAYS of one ISO week is penalised across the veg slots, so a soya gravy on Monday pushes the week's other soya dishes into the following week. MEDIUM, below the same-day rule above, because the client asked to 'try and avoid it' over a week where the same-day case was stated flatly. Scoped to the veg slots rather than the whole plate on purpose: nonveg_main serves chicken on nearly every day of nearly every week by mandate, so a plate-wide week rule would spend its whole budget on a repeat no counter can avoid and would stop discriminating between the ones it can. scope:week rather than horizon because the horizon count silently tightens as the plan grows -- the defect note 26 fixed for `max`.
rules.name: veg_week_protein_variety

rules._comment: The plate should not be all one texture. Five saucy dishes out of six satisfies every other rule in the system and every diner notices it is mushy, and nothing in the solver looked at texture at all. Thresholds and slot set MIRROR src/explain/checks.py::check_texture_contrast (MIN_DISTINCT_TEXTURES, MAX_ONE_TEXTURE_SHARE, MAIN_COURSES) on purpose: that check is the regression test for this rule, and two copies of a threshold are two things that can disagree. Measured achievable before it was written — across all 80 counters the best reachable dominant share is a median of 20% (worst 33%) against this 60% cap, and every counter can reach three distinct textures, so the flags this answers are avoidable rather than forced (the pool-availability test of note 33, which this check had never been put through). SOFT because texture is largely a property of the SLOT, not a free choice: veg_gravy is 98% saucy, starter 89% crisp, dal 88% saucy. A counter serving gravy + dal + non-veg is structurally saucy-heavy, and a hard cap there would trade the day's gravy for a texture score.
rules.name: plate_texture_spread

rules._comment: A 5-dish non-veg lunch station: biryani + chicken gravy + chicken dry + kebab + egg, every day. Gated to counters configured with 5 nonveg_main so it is inert elsewhere, and nonveg_main_daily_pair is capped at 4 so the two never compose the same counter. The five components must land on five DISTINCT dishes, and because the components are >= bounds one dish satisfying two of them frees a cell for a duplicate: the kebab (tandoori_murgh_lababdar) also carries is_nonveg_gravy, and egg curries carry it too, so the station came back with two eggs and no chicken gravy. The gravy and dry components therefore exclude both egg and the tandoor flags, leaving each component one role only. L&T's printed menu has separate 'Non Veg Gravey', 'Non VEG Dry', 'Chicken Kabab' and 'Egg Items' rows, which is exactly this shape.
rules.name: nonveg_main_five_dish

rules._comment: Paneer belongs on a mix / south / north day; chinese and biryani days are the fallback, not the default (client rule, all cities). SOFT on purpose: the hard equivalent is selector_frequency.allowed_day_types, which forbids paneer on the other days outright — and a counter themed chinese or biryani every weekday would then never serve paneer at all. `holiday` (a weekend day on a serve_weekends counter) is not in the preferred list either, so paneer lands on a working day.
rules.name: paneer_prefers_mix_south_north_days

rules._comment: No soya, baby corn, chole or mushroom on a paneer day (client rule, all cities) — they read as substitutes for each other, so serving two wastes a slot. Counted across every slot because the point is the day's plate: a paneer gravy next to a soya veg dry is exactly the pairing to avoid. 'chole' is selected as the chana-gravy family (is_chana_gravy) since that is how the ontology files chole in both cities; the flag also covers the other whole-legume gravies, which fits the intent. Pune carries no mushroom dish, so that part of the selector is simply inert there. Baby corn is matched on the NAME, not on key_ingredient: that column tags 67 Bangalore rows baby_corn of which only 3 are baby-corn dishes (it is the de-facto default for a mixed salad, incl. iceberg_lettuce and black_olives) while the 34 dishes actually named after baby corn are tagged corn / bell_pepper / cauliflower. A HARD rule on that column would ban nearly every salad from paneer days and still miss 31 of the 34 real dishes. A dish matching BOTH sides (chole_paneer) counts as paneer only — see SameDayExclusionRule._hits.
rules.name: paneer_not_with_soya_babycorn_chole_mushroom
